title: Capacity cushion profiles and sticky fallbacks (PRD sketch)
content:
Summary:
This is a working sketch for a complementary set of controls aimed at improving Dedicated capacity resilience and predictability: 1) capacity cushion profiles (pre-configured headroom/eviction behavior per reservation class) and 2) sticky fallback lanes (per-customer affinity lanes for degraded execution when reserved capacity is constrained). The focus is operational simplicity for Platform/SEs while giving product teams predictable latency/cost tradeoffs.

Motivation / Problem:
- Customers buying Dedicated capacity expect stable latency and predictable unit economics. In practice, demand spikes and model hotness cause either higher latency or expensive fallbacks.
- Current options are coarse: hard eviction or blunt throttles. We need softer, observable transitions that preserve experience for the majority of traffic and avoid noisy neighbor cascades.
- Engineering needs a small set of knobs that map to real economic outcomes (cost per token, latency tail, SLO violation rate) without requiring customers to manage low-level pools.

Goals:
- Provide 3 standard capacity cushion profiles customers can pick (Conservative | Balanced | Aggressive). Each maps to headroom %, preemption window, and fallback behavior.
- Implement sticky fallback lanes so that when a request is not served by reserved capacity it can be routed to a warm fallback with affinity to the same tenant/model variant to preserve KV cache effectiveness.
- Ensure graceful soft-preemption: long-running KV/attention-heavy requests should be allowed to finish when possible; short requests can be shed first.
- Surface clear telemetry and cost delta estimates for each profile.

Non-goals:
- Replacing full-blown predictive autoscalers (we integrate with the autoscaler but do not attempt to predict workload patterns here).
- Fine-grained per-API-key micro-quotas (we operate at reservation/tenant level).

Design sketch:
1) Capacity cushion profiles (user-facing):
   - Conservative: +35% headroom, preemption window 120s, fallback type = sticky-warm, billing multiplier 1.0x. Prioritizes latency SLOs and minimizes fallbacks.
   - Balanced: +15% headroom, preemption window 45s, fallback type = sticky-warm then shared-ephemeral, billing multiplier 0.9x. Good tradeoff for standard workloads.
   - Aggressive: +0–5% headroom, preemption window 15s, fallback type = shared-ephemeral, billing multiplier 0.8x. Optimized for cost; accepts more fallbacks and potential tail latency.

   Each profile controls: reserved buffer (extra capacity kept idle), preemption order (by request cost estimate), warm pocket retention time, and fallback priority order.

2) Sticky fallback lanes:
   - Mechanism: maintain a small set of warm fallback instances per reservation that are lightweight (reduced concurrency, preloaded model KV where possible). Requests failing admission in primary pool are routed to these warm lanes if session cookies/affinity token matches and latency budget allows.
   - Affinity semantics: soft affinity token attached to customer requests; token persists across short bursts (~10–60s). Affinity increases effective KV cache hit probability on fallback.
   - Billing: fallbacks bill at reserved token rate but with a small surcharge when using cross-region fallback. For Aggressive profile, fallback falls to cheaper shared-ephemeral pricing.

3) Soft preemption handshake (operational):
   - Preemption signals are annotated with reason and graceful timeout. Frontend will attempt: (a) accelerate short requests to completion, (b) for long-running streams send a suggested pause point (checkpoint) and migrate to fallback or queue.
   - If migration occurs, sticky token attempts to preserve KV state where possible (best-effort).

Admission & routing rules (high level):
   - Requests evaluated by estimated token cost and tail risk (derived from historical percentiles).
   - Low-cost, high-frequency requests get admission preference in Conservative/Balanced. Long, expensive requests may be gated or queued when headroom low.
   - On admission failure: try sticky fallback -> try shared-ephemeral fallback -> reject (with informative quota/fallback header).

API / control plane changes:
   - New reservation config block: capacity_cushion_profile: [conservative|balanced|aggressive] and fallback_policy: [sticky_prefer|cost_prefer].
   - Status endpoints expose current headroom, warm-lane occupancy, recent fallback rate, and per-minute cost delta estimate.

Observability & success metrics:
   - Primary: 99th percentile token latency (by reservation), fallback rate (requests/sec and percent), SLO breach count after fallback, cost-per-1000-tokens delta vs baseline.
   - Secondary: KV cache hit rate on fallback lanes, average warm-lane retention, preemption handshakes per hour, number of customer complaints escalated to SE.

Operational playbook (for SRE/Support):
   - If a reservation has fallback-rate > 5% sustained for 30m in Conservative profile, trigger SE outreach / suggest step-up of reserved capacity or switching profile.
   - Automatic cool-down: if fallback rate spikes abruptly, system will temporarily increase warm-lane retention and open a small temporary prewarm credit (configurable by org-level policy) for 10–30m.

Telemetry experiments and A/B plan:
   - Canary 1 (internal): enable Balanced profile for 20 internal orgs, measure % fallbacks, latency tail, and cost delta over 7 days.
   - Canary 2 (pilot customers): opt-in for three small enterprise customers representing different workloads (chatty vs batch). Collect qualitative SE feedback.

Cost and accounting notes:
   - Cushion profiles shift cost exposure between Redwood and customers. Conservative profile increases cost to Redwood if we keep more idle GPUs; we compensate via higher reservation price. Pricing multipliers above are placeholders.
   - Need billing team to decide surcharge rules for sticky-warm fallback vs shared-ephemeral. Proposal: sticky-warm billed at reservation rate but counted against reservation usage; shared-ephemeral billed at host-rate and optionally credited against committed usage if enabled.

Edge cases & open questions:
   - Affinity leakage risk: how long should tokens live? Tradeoff: longer increases cache hits but can cause unfairness.
   - Model variants: when a fallback model is a lower-capacity variant (quantized), how to surface quality regression risk and allow auto-rollbacks?
   - Security: do sticky lanes need stricter tenancy checks? Likely yes; fallback lanes must enforce reservation-scoped encryption keys and audit trails.

Next steps / To-do:
   - Sync with Billing to finalize pricing multipliers and fallback billing semantics (owner: Lina).
   - Prototype sticky token and warm-lane lifecycle in canary infra (owner: Darius).
   - Define acceptance criteria for canary: fallback rate < 2% on Balanced for internal orgs, KV hit lift >= 15% on fallback lanes, 99p latency within 1.2x baseline.

Notes to self / rough ideas (informal):
   - Might be useful to provide a ’custom cushion’ mode for large enterprises where they can author a rule DSL (but postpone).
   - Consider exposing an SLO-resilience scorecard in Console that recommends cushion profile based on historical spikes.

Attachments / referenced docs:
- Confluence design sketch: CONFLUENCE-1234 (linked)
- Jira epic: JIRA-DED-987
- Ops playbook stub: github.com/redwood-inference/ops/patch/2345

End of sketch.

-- Ava (draft)
